findings.message: The loop body (cell 3 lines 6–10) is forward, loss, loss.backward(), optimizer.step(), and the optimizer is a stock optim.Adam (cell 3 line 3). No line in the notebook calls optimizer.zero_grad() or model.zero_grad(). PyTorch adds to .grad on every backward(), so from the second batch onward each Adam step uses the sum of all gradients seen so far instead of the current batch's gradient. This follows from statement order inside one cell and does not depend on notebook execution order. Runtime qualification: it changes the result only when the loader yields at least two batches, i.e. more than 32 training rows; the row count of features.npz is unresolved.
findings.suggestion: Call optimizer.zero_grad() at the top of the loop body, before the forward pass.
findings.title: Training loop never clears gradients between optimizer steps

findings.message: Inside cell 2, line 2 calls scaler.fit_transform(X) on the full array and lines 3–4 split X_scaled afterwards, so the scaler's mean and variance include the rows that end up in X_test. Both statements live in the same cell, so this order holds in every successful execution of cell 2 and does not depend on notebook execution order. Qualifications: (1) realized impact depends on downstream use. In this notebook X_test and y_test are never read again; the only consumer of the split is cell 3 line 4, which uses X_train and y_train, so no leaked metric is computed here. The leak becomes material once X_test is evaluated or the fitted scaler is reused, and the training features are in any case standardized with test-row statistics. (2) Under the literal single-session reading of the recorded order, cell 2 would fail on line 2 before anything is fitted, so this is a property of the code, not a confirmed event in the recorded session.
findings.suggestion: Split first, then fit on the training rows only: scaler.fit(X_train), then scaler.transform(X_train) and scaler.transform(X_test); or wrap the scaler and estimator in a Pipeline.
findings.title: StandardScaler is fitted on all rows before the train/test split

findings.message: Observed in the notebook JSON: execution_count is 1 for cell 0, 2 for cell 2, 3 for cell 1 and 4 for cell 3 (JSON lines 15, 40, 28, 58), so the recorded order is cell 0 → cell 2 → cell 1 → cell 3 while the source order is 0 → 1 → 2 → 3. Cell 2 reads X and y (lines 2–4), whose only bindings in the notebook are cell 1 lines 4–5. What this means depends on runtime state the file does not record. (a) Literal reading, one kernel session with sources unchanged since they ran: In[1] is the first execution after kernel start and belongs to cell 0 (imports only), so at In[2] the names X and y are unbound and cell 2 line 2 would raise NameError; X_train and y_train would then be unbound and cell 3 line 4 would fail at In[4] too. The saved file neither confirms nor refutes this, because every cell has outputs: [] and so stores no traceback and no success output. (b) If the saved sources differ from what actually ran (cells edited or split after execution, for example code at In[1] that also bound X and y), cell 2 may have scaled and split arrays bound by code that is no longer in the file; the reload at In[3] then rebinds X and y without refreshing X_scaled or X_train, so training at In[4] would use splits derived from older arrays rather than from the most recently loaded data. Merely moving cells after running them would not create this state. (c) If the counters come from more than one kernel session, they do not describe one chronological run at all, and each kernel restart would have discarded earlier bindings. (d) The counters may be hand-authored: the file lives under analyzer/tests/fixtures and is named leak_out_of_order. These readings cannot be told apart without execution history. A top-to-bottom run follows source order, where load precedes scale/split, and has none of these hazards.
findings.suggestion: Restart the kernel and Run All so the counters match source order before trusting any result from this notebook, and keep load → scale/split → train in dependency order.
findings.title: Recorded execution counters put the scale/split cell before the data-load cell

findings.message: torch.tensor(X_train) and torch.tensor(y_train) inherit NumPy dtypes (cell 3 line 4), and nn.Linear(10, 3) hard-codes 10 input features and 3 classes (cell 3 line 1). nn.Linear parameters default to float32, and CrossEntropyLoss with class-index targets expects int64 labels in [0, 3). Whether model(features) and criterion(outputs, labels) succeed therefore depends on what features.npz holds: float64 features (StandardScaler keeps float64 and converts integer input to float64) would raise a dtype mismatch at the forward pass; labels that are not int64 or fall outside [0, 3) would fail at the loss; a feature width other than 10 would fail in the Linear layer. features.npz is not in the workspace and nothing was executed, so this is an unresolved risk, not an observed failure. The library behaviour cited here is general knowledge of PyTorch and scikit-learn, not something read from workspace source.
findings.suggestion: Make the contract explicit: torch.tensor(X_train, dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(y_train, dtype=torch.long), and derive in_features and the class count from X.shape[1] and the label set, or assert them right after loading.
findings.title: Tensor dtypes and the 10-feature / 3-class shape depend on the absent features.npz
